transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-01-28 14:23 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood Solutions), Maya Singh (NovaHealth SRE), Ethan Park (NovaHealth Security), Daniel Ruiz (NovaHealth ML Platform)

Summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect):
Redwood walked through private VPC deployment pattern; we discussed interface endpoints (PrivateLink), NAT/egress rules, DNS split-horizon for model downloads and telemetry, and how network design affects runtime behavior for KV cache and batching. Customer asked about cross-account endpoints and peeking at p99 latency for 8k/16k contexts. Action items captured at end.

00:00:00 Lena: okay hi everybody thanks for joining, this is Lena from Redwood, i think we have Marcus and Priya on from our side as well. can you quick introduce?
00:00:08 Maya: hi maya here, lead SRE at NovaHealth. we run most of our infra in a dedicated AWS account and we are evaluating private deployments for PHI workloads.
00:00:15 Ethan: ethan, security architect. main concerns are KMS integration, private egress, audit logging.
00:00:21 Daniel: daniel, ml platform, want to understand runtime perf and how model artifacts are distributed into our VPC.
00:00:28 Marcus: great thanks. quick agenda: networking (privatelink, endpoints, peering), dns/route tables, then runtime implications (latency/kv cache/batching/quant), then perf plan.

00:02:05 Priya: quick callout, our Private deployment is basically a control plane in Redwood cloud and a data path served out of the customer's VPC via interface endpoints or dedicated machines — so traffic for inference can stay inside the VPC and not traverse public internet.
00:02:23 Maya: is that via PrivateLink or do you do VPC peering?
00:02:26 Marcus: we support both patterns. PrivateLink (interface endpoints) is our recommended for cross-account isolation — you create an interface endpoint in your VPC that points to a Redwood endpoint service. it avoids route-table-level peering complexity.
00:02:44 Ethan: cross-account PrivateLink sounds good, but what about ENI limits? we have high concurrency workloads and worry about running out of ENIs on small subnets.
00:02:53 Marcus: good question. ENI scaling and subnet IP exhaustion are real. we recommend sizing subnets for expected burst concurrency and using multiple AZs. typical guidance: leave room for model worker ENIs + interface endpoints + other infra. we can share the recommended IP budget doc.
00:03:12 Maya: do you require public IP egress for model downloads or for telemetry?
00:03:17 Priya: we usually do model artifact distribution over an internal artifact store — there are two options: Redwood can pull model artifacts through a PrivateLink-controlled channel so no public egress, or the customer can allow egress to our artifact S3 endpoint using VPC endpoints. both work. telemetry and control-plane calls can be routed over PrivateLink.
00:03:38 Daniel: latency wise, what's the expected additional ms for PrivateLink vs direct public?
00:03:42 Marcus: PrivateLink usually adds a small extra hop but keeps traffic inside the AWS network; often p95 delta is single digit milliseconds compared to public internet TO the same region; the big factors are AZ placement and whether model I/O hits a remote storage system.
00:04:10 Maya: we need p99 numbers though, our SLOs are tight.
00:04:14 Marcus: agreed — that's why we propose a benchmark run inside your VPC that exercises 1) cold start (model load), 2) steady-state streaming with batching, 3) KV cache hit/miss patterns. we'll capture p50/p95/p99 for token latencies and end-to-end request time.

00:07:55 Ethan: about NAT gateway vs egress-only, we prefer minimizing NAT costs and want strict egress controls. can Redwood operate fully with no IGW/NAT, entirely through PrivateLink and interface endpoints?
00:08:06 Priya: yes, you can operate without NAT for inference traffic. model serving and control-plane calls over PrivateLink + interface endpoints; for managed updates we may need outbound access for the initial artifact sync unless you host artifacts in a reachable VPC endpoint. so either you host model artifacts in your S3 with gateway endpoints or we provide an interface endpoint to our artifact service.
00:08:27 Maya: what's the DNS story? we run split-horizon and private hosted zones. will the endpoint resolve internally?
00:08:33 Marcus: PrivateLink uses interface endpoints with ENIs in your subnets; DNS can be auto-resolved (AWS can create an internal DNS name that resolves to the interface endpoint). If you use split-horizon private zones, you might need to update or add zone records. we support providing the exact hostnames to add to your private hosted zone if needed.
00:09:05 Daniel: if we use VPC endpoints, what's the TLS termination model and certs?
00:09:10 Priya: for interface endpoints with PrivateLink, TLS is end-to-end — Redwood terminates TLS on our service side. we can support mutual TLS if you want mTLS, or we can terminate and validate client certs. for cert management we integrate with customer KMS for key wrapping and can accept customer-managed certs for mutual auth.

00:12:42 Marcus: shifting to runtime — KV cache: we maintain an in-memory KV cache per model worker for prefix caches. the cache is memory-resident and benefits greatly from locality; network jitter can hurt throughput because cache misses cause longer tails due to remote weight loads or disk pulls.
00:12:58 Daniel: do you shard the KV cache across workers or is it per process?
00:13:02 Marcus: per worker primarily; we do cross-worker sharing only when configured with a shared cache tier — that usually adds network overhead and is recommended for very large multi-model clusters. for most private deployments per-worker KV cache is the lowest-latency option.
00:13:18 Daniel: so network design matters for cache warmup and model pulls. how do quantized models change the picture?
00:13:24 Marcus: quantized models are smaller so artifact transfer is faster and memory footprint is lower; that reduces cold-start time. however quantized kernels sometimes have different CPU/GPU memory access patterns which interact with batch sizes. you might see slightly different latency/throughput tradeoffs; we recommend running quantized vs fp16 benches.

00:16:40 Maya: batching — we need deterministic latency for interactive features, but also cost constraints. how do you tune batching in Private deployments?
00:16:47 Marcus: Redwood runtime supports continuous batching with latency SLO caps; you configure max batch size and max delay (ms). in private VPC we can tune the batcher aggressively because network variability is lower. but if you have heterogeneous request sizes or you do a lot of long-context calls, you may want smaller max delays. we'll show suggested configs in the perf plan.

00:21:05 Ethan: about metrics and logs — can those be sent to our logging endpoint without leaving the VPC?
00:21:11 Priya: yes, logs and traces can be forwarded via PrivateLink to a customer's telemetry endpoint (e.g., a collector in their VPC). we support sending OpenTelemetry spans to a customer endpoint. audit logs for requests can also be stored in your S3 via gateway endpoint so nothing leaves the VPC.

00:25:40 Daniel: one operational concern — during model rollouts, we want canary traffic and quick rollback. how does that interact with PrivateLink routing?
00:25:48 Marcus: we control routing in the control plane; rollout policies are configured in the control plane and we orchestrate routing to different model worker clusters. from the VPC perspective, endpoints continue to point to Redwood service; we will migrate worker backends behind the endpoint. no extra network changes needed.

00:30:12 Maya: anything special about MTU or fragmentation for large payload streaming?
00:30:18 Marcus: keep MTU at standard 1500; we generally use HTTP/2 streaming; we haven't seen fragmentation become a production problem. if you have nonstandard MTU you should test, but PrivateLink behaves like regular ENI traffic.

00:33:00 Priya: security notes — we support SAML SSO for console, SSO and RBAC for keys; audit logs are immutable and we offer integration with your SIEM via PrivateLink. We also provide a security pack doc (we will share).

00:39:15 Marcus: perf plan recap: we'll run three scenarios inside your VPC: small interactive streams (avg 64 tokens), long-contexts (8k/16k) to show kv cache behavior, and batch throughput (100 concurrent streams). collect p50/p95/p99 token and request latencies, GPU utilization, memory, and network egress.
00:39:38 Ethan: for p99 we need < 300ms for short interactions, is that feasible?
00:39:44 Marcus: likely yes for 2-4k context models with proper batch config and warmed cache on dedicated GPUs; we'll validate with the benchmark run. quantization may help hit cost targets.

00:45:05 Maya: can you give a quick example of a Terraform module? what resources do we create?
00:45:11 Priya: typical module includes: interface endpoint resources (aws_vpc_endpoint), security group for endpoint, route table entries if needed, private hosted zone records, IAM policy for cross-account endpoint acceptance, and optional S3 gateway endpoint if hosting artifacts locally. we'll send a skeleton.

00:51:20 Daniel: network egress for model artifact updates — if we do not want any public egress, what's required?
00:51:26 Marcus: host artifacts in your S3 with gateway endpoint or request Redwood to expose an interface endpoint for artifact service. we can also do an initial bootstrap over an out-of-band secure channel if needed.

00:57:00 Lena: quick recap and next steps — Marcus will prepare perf plan and Terraform skeleton; Lena will send pricing and SOC2/ISO docs; Maya/Ethan will share topology and KMS details. any other questions?
00:57:18 Maya: nope that covers it, thanks.
00:57:22 Ethan: thanks everyone.
00:57:25 Lena: thanks, we'll follow up with notes and schedule the perf run.

End transcript.
